name: Yusuf Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I lead a distribution crew in the city, so it's the poles on the street and the cables under it. A normal day starts at seven at the Eastside yard: we load the truck, check the outage list, and then it's maybe a burnt-out transformer behind a row of shops, then a cable fault in an underground vault where you're kneeling in water with a headlamp. When a storm comes through, normal goes out the window and we work sixteen-hour shifts until the last street has its lights back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the moment the lights come back on and somebody leans out of a window and claps. That still gets me after thirty years. What wears me out is the traffic, honestly, and the night callouts, which my wife Leila tolerates because she's a nurse and keeps worse hours than I do. My daughter Samira is in her second year as an apprentice lineworker at the same company, so now I worry about two of us on the poles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that noise for a better spell-checker. At work it would be a joke for about a week. Online I'd share some article about the bubble bursting and get into an argument with my nephew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, which at fifty-eight is not bad news. I'd finish my last few years leading the crew and hand over to someone good. Samira gets her career the way I had mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd still use the chatbot on my phone for the odd thing, and I'd keep pushing on the safety committee about staffing levels, which is the real fight anyway. Leila and I would keep paying into the pension and keep the flat rented out like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit flat. Like a big match that ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Karim set it up on my phone. I use it to translate the safety bulletins for one of my crew, Tomasz, whose English is still coming along, and to tidy up the bits I write for the union newsletter. It's handy, but it's never once fixed a cable fault for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Samira say if this happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be relieved. She told me last month that some lads at college were saying robots would take the job before she qualified. In this picture she can ignore them.

S0.say: He'd joke that it was all noise for a better spell-checker and share an article about the bubble bursting online. At work it would be a joke for about a week.
S0.think: He thinks nothing changes for him, which at fifty-eight is not bad news. His daughter gets her career in the trade the way he had his.
S0.do: Carries on leading the crew and using a phone chatbot for translations and newsletter writing. Keeps pushing on the safety committee about staffing and keeps paying into the pension while renting out the family flat.
S0.feel: Fine and a bit flat, like a big match that ends nil-nil.
S0.quote: It's handy, but it's never once fixed a cable fault for me.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf is warm, funny and very family-centred, with a daughter now in the same trade. He uses AI for small practical jobs and sees it as handy but not essential. The real fight in his mind is staffing on the safety committee, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we have unions: change is coming, so let's make sure it comes with training and not with pink slips. I'd say it at the yard and at the branch meeting. Online I'd say the companies saving money should pay for the retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fine. I've got the skill and the years, and they'll always need someone who knows the old cables under the city, because half of them aren't even on the maps. Samira's the one I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the first course for whatever new kit comes in, once a couple of other crews had tried it and the bugs were out. I'd ask the union to get apprentices onto the new robot and sensor training early, so they're the ones running it. I'd keep our savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for my girl, but okay for me. It's a change I can see the edges of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn new tools yourself, or leave that to the younger ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn them, but not first. I'm not the guy who wants the shiny new thing on day one, I've seen too many gadgets fail in the rain. But when the crew next door says it works, I'm in, and I'd rather understand it than have some twenty-year-old explain my own job to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Samira to do differently in her apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to put her hand up for anything with sensors or robots, and to keep the climbing and the hand skills too. I'd tell her: be the one who can fix the robot and also fix what the robot can't. She'd roll her eyes, but she'd do it.

S1.say: He'd say this is why unions exist: change is coming, so it should come with training and not pink slips. He'd argue the companies saving money should pay for retraining.
S1.think: He thinks he's fine, with the skill and years and knowledge of old unmapped city cables. His daughter is the one he'd think about.
S1.do: Signs up for training on new kit once other crews have tried it and the bugs are out. Asks the union to get apprentices onto robot and sensor training early, and leaves the family savings as they are.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy for his daughter but okay for himself, since it's a change he can see the edges of.
S1.quote: I'd tell her: be the one who can fix the robot and also fix what the robot can't.
S1.fieldNote: Classic steady adopter: he waits for the crew next door to prove it, then jumps in. He frames retraining as something the union and companies should organise collectively. His advice to his daughter is practical and tender at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should have seen this coming and now it has to step in hard: income support, a pause on layoffs, something. At the branch I'd be calling for an emergency meeting in the first week. Online I'd probably lose my temper more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd lose sleep. Not for me, I've got savings and the flat, but Samira would be halfway through an apprenticeship for a job that might not exist by the time she finishes. I spent thirty years telling her this was the safe trade, and in two years I'd be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Leila and the kids and go through what we've got: the savings, the pension, the flat. We'd tell them the flat is theirs if they need it, rent-free. I'd stop any big spending, put more aside, and go to every union and political meeting I could to push for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, which I'm not used to. I'm the dad, I'm supposed to have the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Samira's the one you'd think about. What about your son, Karim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim tests software for a bank. He'd be hit first, maybe before Samira. He's already said the AI does half his test scripts now. So in this picture I'd have both of them in trouble at the same time, which is the bit that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would you spend money on first, and how much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids first, always. If one of them needed to retrain or move, I'd put up maybe twenty thousand from savings, and Leila would agree without me even asking. The new car I've been wanting would go straight off the list.

S2.say: He'd say the government should have seen it coming and must step in hard with income support or a pause on layoffs. He'd call for an emergency union meeting in the first week.
S2.think: He'd lose sleep, not for himself but because his daughter would be halfway through an apprenticeship for a job that may not exist. His son's software testing job would be hit even sooner.
S2.do: Sits down with his family in the first month to go through savings, pension and the rental flat, offering the flat to his children rent-free. Cuts big spending, saves more, sets aside about twenty thousand to help a child retrain, and goes to union and political meetings to push for income support.
S2.feel: Scared, which he isn't used to, because as the dad he feels he should have the answer.
S2.quote: I spent thirty years telling her this was the safe trade, and in two years I'd be wrong.
S2.fieldNote: His own finances are fine, but both of his adult children would be hit at once, and that's what turns him from calm to sleepless. The line about telling his daughter for thirty years that this was the safe trade carries real guilt. He blames government planning, not the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's not waste them shouting. At the branch I'd push for a deal on retraining with dates and money attached. With friends I'd say it's coming, plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's okay, I'd likely be retired by the time it really lands. For the kids it's still big, but now there's room to turn the ship. Five years is enough for Samira to qualify and pick up something else alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay till sixty-two as planned. I'd help Samira find out which parts of the work stay human longest, maybe robot maintenance, maybe grid control, and help pay for a course if she wanted one. I'd get better at the AI tools myself, so I could help her and Karim understand what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry with a plan attached. That makes it bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Samira would be qualified by 2031. Does that help or hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. She'd be a qualified lineworker, so she'd have a skill to sell, but also a skill that's about to be done by machines. I'd want her to have something next to it by then, like a ticket for working on the robots themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last time you said you'd lose sleep. Would you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some nights, maybe. But it'd be the kind where I lie there making lists, not the kind where I lie there with my heart going. Leila would tell me to go to sleep and make the list in the morning.

S3.say: He'd say there are a few years, so let's not waste them shouting, and push the union for a retraining deal with dates and money. He'd tell friends it's coming and to plan for it.
S3.think: He'd likely be retired when it lands, so he's okay. For his children it's still big, but five years gives room to turn the ship.
S3.do: Stays until sixty-two as planned and helps his daughter find work that stays human longest, offering to pay for a course. Gets better at AI tools himself so he can help both children understand what's coming.
S3.feel: Worried, but it's a worry with a plan attached, which makes it bearable.
S3.quote: But it'd be the kind where I lie there making lists, not the kind where I lie there with my heart going.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn his fear into list-making. He still centres everything on his children, and his own adaptability rises: he'd learn the tools to help them. The difference between lying awake making lists and lying awake with his heart going is a neat way he measures his own stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do this properly: a public plan, retraining for everyone, and the money from all this productivity shared out instead of hoarded. I'd say it at the branch and I'd vote for whoever promised it. Online I'd keep it polite, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, almost nothing, I'd be retired and on my allotment with Leila nagging me about my back. Ten years is the difference between my daughter having a career and my daughter having a warning. She'd be thirty-six, so she'd have time to make a second move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at sixty-two and keep using the AI tools enough to stay sharp. I'd help Samira and Karim build a plan, maybe a second trade each, and offer the flat as a safety net. I'd stay active in the retired members' group to push for the law I talked about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little stone in my shoe about the kids. I'd feel lucky with my timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What would you say to someone just starting an apprenticeship now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to go for it, but go in with your eyes open. Learn the hands-on work, but learn the machines too, and keep your union card in your wallet. The robots will need somebody to blame when the city goes dark, and it might as well be a person who knows what they're doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned the flat a few times. Would you do anything with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep it, for the kids. If things got bad, I'd rather they had a roof than I had the rent. Leila and I have talked about it. It was my mother's, she'd want it used that way.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is time to do it properly: a public plan, retraining for everyone and productivity gains shared out rather than hoarded. He'd vote for whoever promised that.
S4.think: For himself almost nothing changes, since he'd be retired. Ten years gives his daughter time for a second career move rather than just a warning.
S4.do: Retires at sixty-two as planned and keeps using AI tools enough to stay sharp. Helps both children plan a second trade, keeps his mother's flat as a safety net for them, and stays active in the retired members' group.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a small stone in his shoe about his children, and lucky with his timing.
S4.quote: Ten years is the difference between my daughter having a career and my daughter having a warning.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he relaxes into his retirement plans but never stops thinking about his children. He keeps the inherited flat as a family safety net, which says a lot about how he sees his role. His progressive views come through as wanting productivity gains shared out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both my kids would be in the firing line at once and I'd be the one without answers. What would help is income support that kicks in fast, before people lose their homes, and real retraining with wages paid while you learn, so a girl halfway through an apprenticeship doesn't just get dropped.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old cables. Half the city is running on stuff laid before I was born, and nobody has proper drawings of it. Whatever comes, somebody has to know where the bodies are buried, so to speak. I hope they write that knowledge down before people like me retire.

headlineQuote: The robots will need somebody to blame when the city goes dark, and it might as well be a person who knows what they're doing.
portrait: Yusuf Costa is a 58-year-old distribution crew leader who has kept a city's lights on for thirty years, from storm shifts to cable faults in flooded vaults. He's warm, funny and active in his union's safety committee, and uses AI tools now and then for translations and newsletter writing. He's financially secure with savings, a pension and his late mother's rented-out flat, so his worries are almost entirely about his daughter, an apprentice lineworker, and his son, a software tester. The two-year AGI picture leaves him sleepless because both children would be hit at once, while more warning time turns that fear into planning and retraining.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries him most, because both of his children would be hit at once and he'd have no answers for them.
whatWouldHelp: Fast income support before people lose their homes, and retraining with wages paid while you learn, so apprentices aren't just dropped.
